headline: The Gate to Hell at the Heart of a Hermetic State
lede: In the Karakum desert of Turkmenistan, a pit of burning methane some 230 feet across has been alight since the early 1970s, the product of a Soviet drilling accident gone wrong. The crater, nicknamed the **Gateway to Hell**, became one of the planet's more surreal tourist curiosities — a flaming void inside one of the world's most closed countries. In 2025, the Turkmen government announced it had finally brought the blaze under control, ending a half-century of accidental fire.
body:
The story of the Darvaza gas crater begins with Soviet pragmatism meeting geological surprise. In 1971, scientists drilling to study methane deposits in the Karakum desert unwittingly pierced an underground gas field. The ground collapsed; poisonous gases began to escape. The solution, as the engineers understood it, was to burn them off. The fire burned for more than fifty years.

At its peak the pit measured roughly 230 feet wide and 100 feet deep — a scale that photographs struggle to convey. The glow visible across the flat desert made the crater, counterintuitively, a draw for the handful of foreign visitors Turkmenistan admitted each year. It had become, by official recognition, a tourist attraction in a country that otherwise offers few openings to the outside world.

The timing of the extinguishment is not merely symbolic. Turkmenistan sits atop some of the world's largest natural gas reserves, and the perpetual combustion of the Darvaza pit represented decades of wasted resource and uncontrolled *methane* emissions — a greenhouse gas many times more potent than carbon dioxide. Taming the crater signals, or at least gestures at, a more deliberate stewardship of what the country has long taken for granted.

The tweet's framing — Turkmenistan as a rabbit hole, as 'the most hermetic country in the world' — is an invitation rather than an argument. The Darvaza crater serves as a useful entry point: a place simultaneously famous globally and accessible to almost no one, a fitting emblem for a state that has made opacity a governing principle.

concepts.definition: A country that severely restricts the movement of people, information, and outside influence across its borders. In practice this means tight visa controls, state monitoring of visitors, and suppression of independent media. Turkmenistan and North Korea are the most frequently cited examples, though analysts differ on which is more closed.

A large, naturally occurring subsurface gas field in Turkmenistan's Karakum desert that was accidentally breached by Soviet drillers in 1971. The resulting crater was set alight to burn off escaping methane and has burned continuously ever since, earning the nicknames 'Gateway to Hell' and 'Door to Hell.'

The deliberate burning of natural gas that cannot be captured or economically used. At Darvaza the combustion was accidental, but the principle is the same. Because methane is a far more potent greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide, burning it off — though wasteful — is considered less damaging than venting it raw into the atmosphere.

fact_check: The tweet describes Turkmenistan as 'the most hermetic country in the world.' North Korea is more widely cited by analysts and press-freedom organisations as the planet's most closed state; Turkmenistan typically ranks alongside or just below it. The superlative is contested rather than clearly wrong.
